passage: Saturday night. Four months in and I finally did the sums on the back of the rent receipt. The new salary looks bigger on paper. But the rent is higher, the commute is two hours a day, and I pay for a cab whenever the train is late. After all that, we are only a little better off each month. Minakshi asked tonight when I last had dinner at home before eight. I could not remember. I keep telling myself the pay was the reason, but I never counted the rent or the two hours. I feel tired and a bit stupid. Tomorrow I'll sit down with the sheet and Minakshi and go through it properly. - Chaitanya

passage:
Zubin: how's the new job? you were so excited about the salary
Kishore: salary is great on paper
Zubin: on paper?
Kishore: rent here is almost double what I paid in Nagpur. and the office is 90 min each way
Zubin: 90??
Kishore: the cheaper areas are far. I only checked the salary when I said yes. didn't even look at rents
Zubin: so what's left each month?
Kishore: did the maths last night. after rent, cabs and eating out because I'm never home to cook... barely more than before
Zubin: ouch
Kishore: and I leave before my son wakes up and get back after he's asleep. weekends I'm just tired
Zubin: that's the part I'd worry about more than the money
Kishore: yeah. I miss them more than I expected 😔
Zubin: want to talk through options this weekend? maybe a closer flat or a hybrid deal with your manager

passage:
Joseph had driven a delivery van in Thodupuzha for five years when an electronics factory in Hosur offered him a supervisor's job with much higher pay.
"Take it," his friend Kishore said. "That money! You'll be rich."
Joseph did the sum in his head: the new salary minus the old. He signed without asking anything else.
In Hosur, rooms near the factory were taken, so he rented one in a town forty minutes away, at twice his old rent. The factory bus left at six. His wife and daughter stayed back in Thodupuzha until the school year ended, so he also paid for trips home every other weekend.
By the third month, he sat down with a notebook. After rent, bus, meals and train tickets, he had only slightly more than before. And he saw his daughter four days a month.
He called Kishore that night. "The number was big. The life is small."

qa.q: How far away was Joseph's rented room from the factory?
qa.a: In a town forty minutes away.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling when he said "The number was big. The life is small"?
qa.a: Joseph felt disappointed and lonely, realising the higher salary barely helped while he saw his daughter only four days a month.

qa.q: What else could Joseph have done before signing?
qa.a: He could have found out rents, commute and travel costs near the factory, and weighed family time along with the salary.

qa.q: How is Joseph's daughter affected by the move?
qa.a: His daughter sees him only four days a month, so she loses much of her time with her father.

grounding: It shows someone attracted by a higher salary who ignores rent and commute, then finds the take-home gain small and family time much reduced.
